patient.chief_complaint: Progressive headaches, left arm weakness, and a new-onset seizure
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Tiffany Coleman is a 64-year-old right-handed woman and high school math teacher who presents to the emergency department after experiencing a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home approximately 2 hours ago. Her wife reports that the seizure lasted roughly 90 seconds and was preceded by her left arm stiffening and shaking for about 15 seconds before becoming generalized. She was post-ictal and confused for approximately 20 minutes before regaining conversational ability, although her wife notes she has still not returned to her baseline. There was no tongue bite or urinary incontinence. She has no prior history of seizures. On further questioning, her wife describes a 3-week history of progressively worsening headaches, initially attributed by their primary care physician to tension-type headaches and treated with ibuprofen. These headaches are worst in the morning upon waking, are dull and pressure-like, and have been accompanied by nausea on several occasions, with two episodes of vomiting over the past week. She also reports that over the past 2 weeks, she has developed noticeable weakness of her left arm, initially manifesting as difficulty buttoning her shirt and clumsiness when writing on the blackboard with her left hand for emphasis. Her colleagues at school remarked that she seemed to be struggling to find the right words during her lectures, something entirely out of character for a woman known for her articulate teaching style. Over the past week, her wife has noticed she seems more forgetful and occasionally confused, once becoming disoriented briefly while driving on a familiar route home from school. She was placed on medical leave from teaching five days ago after an episode where she lost her train of thought mid-sentence during a parent-teacher conference. She denies recent fever, chills, night sweats, or significant weight loss, although her wife thinks she may have lost a few pounds over the past month due to decreased appetite from the nausea.

tissue_diagnosis.impression: Integrated diagnosis: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4. results.title: Radiotherapy plus Concomitant and Adjuvant Temozolomide for Glioblastoma
results.authors: Stupp R, Mason WP, van den Bent MJ, et al.
results.key_finding: The Stupp protocol established the standard of care: maximal safe surgical resection followed by concurrent radiotherapy (60 Gy in 30 fractions) with daily temozolomide (75 mg/m2), then 6 cycles of adjuvant temozolomide (150-200 mg/m2, days 1-5 of each 28-day cycle). Median overall survival improved from 12.1 to 14.6 months.

results.title: Effect of Tumor-Treating Fields Plus Maintenance Temozolomide vs Maintenance Temozolomide Alone on Survival in Patients With Glioblastoma: A Randomized Clinical Trial (EF-14)
results.authors: Stupp R, Taillibert S, Kanner A, et al.
results.key_finding: Addition of tumor-treating fields (TTFields) to maintenance temozolomide improved median overall survival to 20.9 months vs 16.0 months. TTFields is now considered part of the standard of care for newly diagnosed GBM.

results.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines: Central Nervous System Cancers, Version 2.2024
results.key_finding: Standard of care for newly diagnosed GBM: maximal safe resection, followed by RT (60 Gy) + concurrent TMZ, then adjuvant TMZ + TTFields. For MGMT unmethylated tumors, temozolomide benefit is reduced but still recommended. Clinical trial enrollment should be offered.

differential.key_features: No known primary cancer; staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis negative; infiltrative margins and corpus-callosum or eloquent-cortex involvement more typical of primary glioma than metastasis
In immunocompetent patients typically presents as homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass with diffuse DWI restriction and no central necrosis; ring enhancement with necrosis argues against
No fever or leukocytosis; DWI restriction at the enhancing rim (not centrally as in pyogenic pus) and elevated rCBV are inconsistent with abscess
Closed ring enhancement, marked mass effect, and central necrosis are atypical for tumefactive MS; demyelinating lesions usually show incomplete ('open') ring enhancement on the cortical side

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of suspected high-grade glioma absent a specific cardiac question (e.g., suspected paraneoplastic endocarditis)
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of a brain mass and adds resource cost without informing management

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected intracranial mass with imaging evidence of herniation: the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. Even when LP is otherwise safe, CSF studies are low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is suspected, to identify mass effect and herniation risk before LP
Imaging plans the approach and identifies the enhancing target to sample; biopsying before it risks a non-diagnostic specimen from a necrotic centre

critical_actions: Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or maximal safe resection) and operative planning
Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Administer dexamethasone (loading dose 10 mg IV, then 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to reduce vasogenic edema given imaging evidence of herniation/significant mass effect
Initiate antiepileptic therapy with levetiracetam (preferred non-enzyme-inducing AED) for documented seizure activity
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type & screen) before craniotomy/biopsy
Plan multimodal treatment per molecular and histological profile (e.g., Stupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation with temozolomide for IDH-wildtype GBM)
Monitor blood glucose closely given anticipated corticosteroid use in a patient with diabetes; adjust antihyperglycemic regimen as needed
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture with herniation risk — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
key_reasoning_points: Combination of progressive headache (worse mornings), new focal neurological deficit, and/or new-onset seizure in an adult is a high-risk presentation requiring urgent contrast-enhanced brain MRI

MRI features of a right hemisphere heterogeneously / ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, perilesional FLAIR-hyperintense edema, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, and mass effect are characteristic of high-grade glioma
Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho/NAA, lipid-lactate) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and help guide biopsy targeting
Significant midline shift / herniation risk mandates urgent dexamethasone and neurosurgical evaluation; lumbar puncture is contraindicated
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue (stereotactic biopsy or surgical resection) with molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, 1p/19q, TERT, H3K27M); imaging alone cannot substitute for histology
For IDH-wildtype GBM, current standard of care is maximal safe resection followed by the Stupp protocol (concurrent radiation + temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide)

Avoid ordering off-pathway advanced-imaging modalities (DaTscan, amyloid PET, FDG-PET, carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler) — they address other neurological differentials and add cost without informing glioma management
New-onset focal or generalized seizure with a focal-onset mass mandates AED therapy (levetiracetam preferred — non-enzyme-inducing, fewer interactions with temozolomide)

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward - classic presentation with progressive headaches, focal neurological deficits, new-onset seizure, and MRI showing a large ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis and midline shift
clinical_pearls: New-onset seizure in an adult older than 40 should always prompt brain imaging to rule out structural pathology, particularly brain tumors
Morning headaches with nausea and vomiting suggest elevated intracranial pressure, a red flag for intracranial mass lesions
Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive primary malignant brain tumor in adults, with a median survival of 14-21 months with optimal therapy
The Stupp protocol (surgery + concurrent chemoradiotherapy + adjuvant temozolomide) remains the standard of care since 2005
MGMT promoter methylation status is the most important molecular predictor of temozolomide response, but treatment is given regardless of methylation status
